series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 7.2 · October 2026
title: A Global Fiscal Indicators Dashboard

slides.title: A Global Fiscal Indicators Dashboard for Climate-Fiscal Analysis
slides.subtitle: Find the binding constraint before choosing the climate-fiscal lever
slides.message: Eighty public indicators for 217 economies on one page, each with its year and source. Four economies show the profile separating a revenue problem from a debt-service problem; a check against the IMF's own files confirms most values and finds three compilation faults.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: Climate-fiscal advice starts with a scramble across a dozen databases

stats.label: indicators in twelve blocks, each block answering one question
public datasets, each with its own country names, units and vintages

slides.text: Debt, tax, capital spending, the cost of capital, fuel subsidies and the power mix sit in different places. Gathering them takes a day per country and a week per region, so advice tends to fix on the first number found.
slides.source: Global Fiscal Indicators dashboard, version 1.3; working paper 7.2, What the dashboard assembles.

slides.title: The dashboard is organized around the questions an adviser asks, not around datasets
rows: IRENA; Steffen et al.; IEA; IDS
Who finances it, and with what risk?
OECD; IDS; PEFA; World Bank PPI
How much fossil money runs through the budget?
IMF WoRLD; IMF subsidy data; BOOST
Does it sell fossil fuels, or buy them?
slides.note: Four assessment blocks carry the diagnosis; three context blocks explain it; five appendices hold reference data.

slides.title: The build is designed so that errors cannot hide

points.text: every value as a row with its country, year and source file (about 130,000 rows; 12,400 latest values).
a missing value stays missing, and the profile counts the gaps by block.
the build halts if its configuration asks for an indicator the data do not supply.

slides.title: Scores rank countries from 1 to 10, and there is deliberately no overall index

points.text: so a few extreme values do not squeeze everyone else into the middle.
7 and above Good, below 4 Bad; context blocks read High, Medium, Low.
a composite "may disguise serious failings in some dimensions" (OECD and JRC 2008).
so read the weakest indicator and the count of missing values.

slides.source: Working paper 7.2, Scoring and evaluation; OECD and JRC (2008).

slides.title: A check against the publishers confirms most values and finds three faults

points.text: "interest-to-revenue" is net interest, and its filter drops net creditors.
Colombia's excises look lowest as a share of revenue, but equal Indonesia's as a share of GDP (1.06 and 1.11%).
the panel's renewable share is 5 to 19 points off Ember's (chart).
